claims.text: Controlled annealing of a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy can induce stable, finely dispersed coherent nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoprecipitates will enhance the radiation tolerance of tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys.
The nanoprecipitate-forming treatment will preserve the mechanical integrity needed for plasma-facing applications.
The initial alloy produced by conventional melt-casting or powder metallurgy has a solid-solution microstructure without significant secondary-phase precipitates.
Annealing at approximately 800°C for 1 hour, followed by controlled cooling, is sufficient to form and stabilize coherent nanoprecipitates.
A controlled cooling rate will limit precipitate coarsening.
An inert annealing atmosphere will preclude oxidation.
The treatment will produce uniformly distributed coherent nanoprecipitates in the HEA matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced point defects and small defect clusters.
Nanoprecipitate interfaces disrupt long-range one-dimensional defect migration.
Nanoprecipitate interfaces promote recombination of radiation-induced defects.
Enhanced defect recombination will reduce void swelling and defect accumulation.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation movement or transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can provide high strength without compromising tensile ductility in a tungsten-based refractory HEA.
Under 150 keV Ar+ irradiation, the annealed alloy will have lower defect density than the untreated baseline.
Under 150 keV Ar+ irradiation, the annealed alloy will exhibit less void swelling than the untreated baseline.
After irradiation, the annealed alloy's tensile strength and ductility will remain comparable to or exceed those of the untreated baseline.
The proposed benefit is expected to hold for irradiation and thermal exposure conditions similar to 150 keV Ar+ irradiation and temperatures near 800°C.

The hypothesis is falsified if treatment fails to produce a statistically significant reduction in both defect density and void swelling, or if post-irradiation mechanical properties deteriorate relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits unspecified minor alloying changes in addition to annealing, whereas the proposed two-group experiment describes the treated group as differing only by annealing. If alloying tweaks are used, the experiment would not isolate the claimed single intervention.
